name: RLC impedance
seoDesc: RLC impedance: work out angular frequency (ω) (RLC in parallel) from the impedance of R, L and C and the angular frequency (ω). A free physics calculator…
summary: angular frequency (ω) (RLC in parallel) is what the RLC impedance calculator works out, and it gets there from the impedance of R, L and C, the angular frequency (ω) and the par zb. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the RLC impedance calculator work?
sections.html:
The RLC impedance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports angular frequency (ω) (RLC in parallel) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the operation); then you type in the impedance of R, L and C (RLC in series), the angular frequency (ω) (RLC in series), the impedance of R, L and C (RLC in parallel) and the par zb.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as RLC in series and RLC in parallel. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in ohms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in radians per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in ohms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the RLC impedance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Angular frequency (ω)=2 × PI × frequency (f)
Frequency (f)=(1 ÷ 2) × angular frequency (ω) ÷ PI
Par zc=par zb + the square root of (-par za + (impedance of R, L and C ^ -2))
Par za=(resistance (R) ^ -2)
Inductance (L)=(1 ÷ 2) ÷ (PI × frequency (f) × par zb)
Frequency (f)=(1 ÷ 2) × par zc ÷ (PI × capacitance (C))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Operation set to RLC in series and Frequency (f) = 10 kHz. Working through the relationship above gives Angular frequency (ω) = 62.83185 rad/s.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Angular frequency (ω) = 62.83185 rad/s should be roughly the size you expected from Operation set to RLC in series and Frequency (f) = 10 kHz.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Inductance – henry, opening in millihenries
  • Capacitance, opening in microfarads
  • Frequency, opening in kilohertz
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Frequency, opening in hertz
  • Rotational speed, opening in radians per second

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The RLC impedance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the impedance of R, L and C, the angular frequency (ω) and the par zb — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the RLC impedance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns angular frequency (ω) (RLC in parallel), derived from the impedance of R, L and C, the angular frequency (ω) and the par zb. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the RLC impedance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the impedance of R, L and C, the angular frequency (ω) and the par zb, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter resistance (R) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Resistance (R) opens in ohms and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Angular frequency (ω) = 62.83185 rad/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the RLC impedance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
